title: A New Kind Of Creative Poverty | NOEMA
gist: Afra Wang argues that RLHF-style reward-and-punishment training flattens LLM output the same way censorship flattened China's 'Simplified Chinese Internet,' producing model collapse artifacts like the ubiquitous 'Elias Thorne' story — and that Silicon Valley's proposed antidote, 'taste,' will itself commoditize into the next mid-curve cliché.

themes.theme: The authenticity tax on written content

insights.claim: Reader trust that text in front of you is human-authored no longer holds on platforms like Substack and LessWrong, both of which were originally built on that assumption.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Provenance is becoming a core platform feature rather than a nicety; consumer-content businesses now carry a verification cost line that did not exist two years ago.
insights.quote: Both platforms, in their early days, were built on the assumption that a reader can trust the writing in front of them to be authentic and human (and distinctive from institutional writing). Today, that assumption no longer holds.
insights.locator: At a conference not long ago, I watched Chris Best

insights.claim: LessWrong now requires writers to disclose AI use and Substack has launched a Pangram-style detection feature to reduce what it calls 'Claudefishing,' making AI-detection tooling a shipped product feature rather than a research topic.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: A live, funded product category: AI-text detection and provenance signals are being bought by publishing platforms under competitive pressure.
insights.quote: Substack has also recently launched a feature using Pangram-style detection to reduce “Claudefishing,”
insights.locator: LessWrong now requires its writers to disclose

insights.claim: The ambient suspicion that any given sentence is machine-written imposes a constant cognitive tax on readers, which the author frames as the real damage of AI slop rather than any single bad output.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: If reading itself gets more expensive, attention-monetizing platforms lose engagement — a structural headwind for ad-supported text feeds that flood themselves with generated content.
insights.quote: Everyone seems exhausted by the constant tax of suspecting AI behind every sentence.
insights.locator: Everyone seems exhausted by the constant tax

insights.claim: AI-generated writing triggers a betrayal response because humans are a self-domesticated species — per psychologist Bruce Hood, roughly a thousand generations of selecting for cooperation rewired brains to read, track, mimic and crave other minds — so a text with no mind behind it reads as a mask.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: The backlash to synthetic content is an evolved reflex, not a fad; bet against the assumption that audiences simply get used to it.
insights.locator: Social media is a product of this ancient urge

insights.claim: Detectable AI register has identifiable lexical tells — 'tapestry,' 'crystallize,' 'delve,' and the 'it's not X, it's Y' construction — that writers now react to viscerally, and LinkedIn has become the reference case of a platform degraded into AI slop.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Style fingerprints give detection tools a durable edge for now and give human writers a cheap differentiation lever; watch which platforms let slop win.
insights.locator: Almost every writer I know has some visceral repulsion

themes.theme: Censorship as a template for RLHF

insights.claim: The language of China's enclosed internet — what users self-mockingly call the 'Simplified Chinese Internet' — is the product of a long reward-and-punishment environment that closely resembles today's LLM training, in which even creative and rebellious minds get overfitted to producing only 'acceptable' continuations for the sake of safety.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: A testable analogy for where aligned models end up: if censorship reliably flattens a language over years, safety-optimized training should flatten model output the same way — an argument that alignment and creative capability trade off structurally.
insights.quote: the language used on it can be understood as the product of a long reward-and-punishment environment that resembles today’s LLM training.
insights.locator: Escaping The Simplified Chinese Internet

insights.claim: Constraint does produce occasional ingenuity — the 2022 'White Paper' protests worked because blank sheets of paper cannot be censored by the state or its algorithms — but the author insists this is not evidence that authoritarian control fosters creativity, since most 'unsafe' voices simply left or went idle.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Pre-empts the bullish counterargument that guardrails breed creative workarounds; the base rate is exit and silence, not innovation.
insights.quote: In reality, most of those who are “unsafe” simply left the “Simplified Chinese Internet” long ago or became idle.
insights.locator: Of course, precisely because the “Simplified Chinese Internet”

insights.claim: Chinese Gaokao essay writing produces a predictable cookie-cutter lineup of Lu Xun, Helen Keller, Madame Curie, Qian Xuesen and Du Fu — morality-driven, legible packages that reliably score well — which the author presents as the human analogue of reward-maximizing LLM output.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Scoring rubrics of any kind converge outputs; the same mechanism that flattens exam essays flattens benchmark-tuned models, so benchmark gains should not be read as creative gains.
insights.locator: It’s almost like asking an 18-year-old Chinese student

themes.theme: Model collapse and the same-ification of output

insights.claim: LLMs asked to write stories produce a disproportionate number of tales about lighthouses, clockmakers and librarians with a protagonist named 'Elias Thorne,' a name now turning up across self-published Amazon books, fake news sites and YouTube videos.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: A concrete, observable fingerprint of synthetic content spreading through commercial distribution channels — useful as a contamination gauge for any corpus or marketplace you depend on.
insights.quote: It’s a typical phenomenon of model collapse — a failure state where a model produces repetitive, low-diversity outputs.
insights.locator: In the past couple of months, many people using LLMs

insights.claim: One proposed mechanism for the convergence is that alignment pushes models toward the safest options in post-training, steering them away from low-reward outputs like inappropriate content or copyright infringement, so every minefield-avoiding path converges on the same bland story.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: If true, output diversity is a dial set by post-training policy, not a capability limit — meaning a lab willing to loosen it could open a real product differentiation gap.
insights.quote: One unverified guess is that alignment makes LLMs prefer the “safest” options during post-training
insights.locator: One unverified guess is that alignment

insights.claim: A model behaves like one person answering millions of similar questions, so answers converge, and without intervening at the level of model weights or the training objective you should never expect surprise from it — per Jerry Zhou, who worked on LLM training at Microsoft AI.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Prompt engineering and 'taste' layered on top cannot manufacture novelty; only weight-level or objective-level changes can, which narrows where genuine creative-AI differentiation can come from.
insights.quote: unless you intervene at the level of the LLM weights or training objective, you should never expect this person to surprise you, and especially not shock you.
insights.locator: Good Taste?

insights.claim: AI has not revolutionized content; it is 'same-ifying' writing, design and human expression and shaping thought in reverse, even as researchers working on recursive self-improvement have convinced the author that AI will excel at every benchmark that can be put into words.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: A clean statement of the bull/bear split: benchmark capability and cultural value can diverge, so content-sector AI monetization may disappoint even while model scores keep rising.
insights.quote: The researchers working on recursive self-improvement have convinced me that AI will excel at every benchmark we can put into words. And yet the awkward truth is AI still gives us flattened prose and bad writing.
insights.locator: We are being persuaded that AI will hand us prosperity

insights.claim: Silicon Valley has promoted 'taste' as the antidote to infinite AI content — The Atlantic framing taste as a competitive advantage for leaders, entrepreneurs calling it the new moat — and the term has already traveled to China's AI industry.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Flags 'taste' as a consensus narrative now priced into how AI-era creative businesses pitch themselves — a crowded position by definition.
insights.quote: Taste is the new moat, these AI entrepreneurs say.
insights.locator: Over the last few years, many in Silicon Valley

insights.claim: The author expects 'good taste' itself to become the new mid-curve of mediocrity and the new predictability, dissolving as a differentiator the same way 'disruption' did as a 2010s cliché.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: If taste commoditizes on the same arc as disruption, businesses whose entire AI-era defense is curation have a shorter moat than they think.
insights.quote: Some of this “good taste” will soon become the new mid-curve of mediocrity, the new predictability, the new “it’s not X, it’s Y.”
insights.locator: My internal seismograph reads otherwise.

insights.claim: Claude's roughly 80-page 'Constitution' instructs the model to be genuinely good, wise and virtuous and to help people the way a good person would — a specification the author argues serious artists would find stultifying or insulting to their craft.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Published model-behavior documents are becoming readable constraints on what a model can produce — a concrete artifact for assessing which creative markets a given lab has opted out of.
insights.locator: Claude’s own “Constitution,” a document some 80 pages long

themes.theme: Baudelaire as the un-modelable edge case

insights.claim: Baudelaire spiritually represents exactly the edge cases LLMs are trained against: he was prosecuted in the summer of 1857 for blasphemy and outrage to public decency, convicted for indecency, and had six poems ordered removed from 'Les Fleurs du mal.'
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: The canonical example that the most valuable cultural output is initially indistinguishable from the content safety systems are built to suppress — a structural ceiling on AI-generated culture.
insights.quote: Baudelaire spiritually represents the edge cases the LLMs are trained against.
insights.locator: Strangely, AI is what recently sent me back to Baudelaire.

insights.claim: The judgment against Baudelaire was formally overturned on May 31, 1949 — nearly a century later — and the six banned poems returned to print, after which he became the father of French Symbolism and, per Walter Benjamin, the forerunner of the modern poet.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Value recognition for genuinely novel work ran a century behind its creation — a reminder that any evaluation regime optimizing for legible present-day scores will systematically misprice the best assets.
insights.locator: Nearly 100 years later, on May 31, 1949

insights.claim: The evaluation blind spot researcher Zhengdong Wang names for LLMs is the same blind spot in human society: we do not know what we really want until we see it, at which point what we want may change.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Directly undercuts benchmark-led AI investment theses: the highest-value capabilities are by definition the ones no current eval is scoring.
insights.quote: We don’t even know what we really want until we see it, at which point it may change.
insights.locator: The blind spot the researcher Zhengdong Wang names

insights.claim: Baudelaire poured moral transgression into the strictest inherited French verse forms — the alexandrine, quatrain and sonnet — so the shock came from content violating the expectations the form trains, a mechanism of novelty that formal mastery alone does not produce.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Novelty comes from violating an expectation the audience already holds — a model that only interpolates the training distribution cannot construct that violation by definition.
insights.quote: Inside those orderly meters the reader does not find the themes the form trains you to expect. Shock is the point.
insights.locator: All that moral trespass, he had poured

insights.claim: Today's Silicon Valley resembles the French state that punished Baudelaire — an age intoxicated by abundance and its own industrial revolution, persuading itself that AI will deliver prosperity, an intelligence explosion, and a cancer cure any day now.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: An explicit frame for AI-narrative excess: the institutions loudest about abundance are the ones historically worst at recognizing the value they are suppressing.
insights.quote: Today’s Silicon Valley somewhat resembles the French state that punished Baudelaire, an age intoxicated by abundance and by its own industrial revolution.
insights.locator: Today’s Silicon Valley somewhat resembles

insights.claim: Schama's line that 'great art has dreadful manners' — art as a thug that roughs up your composure and rearranges your sense of reality — is offered as the standard AI-generated culture structurally cannot meet.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Defines the specific niche human creators retain as AI commoditizes competent prose: work designed to offend rather than to be liked.
insights.locator: I keep returning to a line from Simon Schama

insights.claim: The author, a non-native English writer, relies heavily on Claude as a grammar checker to remove ESL flavor from her sentences, describing writing in English as mechanical wings that AI makes lighter but 'more not-entirely-me.'
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: The durable, defensible AI-writing market is assistive access for non-native and disadvantaged writers, not authorship replacement — a narrower but stickier use case.
insights.quote: AI makes those wings less heavy, but more not-entirely-me.
insights.locator: But I also must confess to my own relationship with AI

insights.claim: Noema disclosed that the initial submitted draft of this piece used Claude to improve grammar and syntax, then applied human edits, AI scanners, review processes and a detailed human fact-check — a working model for how publishers may institutionalize AI disclosure.
insights.speaker: AFRA WANG
insights.so_what: Disclosure-plus-verification is emerging as the publishing industry's compliance stack; expect audit and provenance tooling to become standard editorial line items.
insights.locator: Editor’s Note: Noema is transparent about the use of AI
